senses: Someone or something that is phenomenal, especially a promising young player in sports like baseball, American football, basketball, tennis, and golf.
One who is hip and fashionable.
ety: Clipping of phenomenon (“remarkable occurrence”). American English, c. 1890s.
examples: Managed and shortstopped by George Wright and full of league stalwarts—Joe Start, Paul Hines, and Jim O'rourke—they also had 1-year-old phenom Monte Ward as primary moundsman (teams now generally used multiple pitchers).
Jones is a pop-culture phenom whose bold antics, outlandish personality, and dazzling looks defied all norms.

senses: Consisting or made of the wood or bark of the beech tree.
ety: From Middle English bechen, from Old English bēċen (“made of beechwood, beechen”), Proto-West Germanic *bōkīn, equivalent to beech + -en. Cognate with Dutch beuken (“beechen”).
examples: Now withered lay the hemlock-sheaves, And one by one with sighing sound Whispering fell the beechen leaves In the wintry woodland wavering.

senses: Degree of ability to lubricate.
Evasiveness; shiftiness.
Lasciviousness; propensity to lewdness.
ety: From French lubricité or its source, Latin lūbricitās.
examples: Though her lubricity made it redundant, Anthea passed him the oil to caress her thighs.

senses: A mixture consisting of egg white and a sweetener, variously mixed with (in western Europe) almonds or (in eastern Europe) hazelnuts or (in US) used without nuts as a filler in candy bars.
A piece of this mixture, typically eaten as a confection.
ety: From French nougat, from Occitan nogat, from noga (“nut”), ultimately from Latin nux (“nut”) + -atus (“-ate, forming adjectives and substantives having or resembling some thing or trait”). Compare Spanish nuégado.
examples: When you make a nougat of large dimensions, put in the almonds a few at a time.

senses: A dense, but generally small, growth of shrubs, bushes or small trees; a copse.
A dense aggregation of other things, concrete or abstract.
ety: Inherited from Middle English *thikket, from Old English þiccet, from þicce (“thick”) + Old English nominal suffix -et. Compare similar German Dickicht (“thicket”), which is first attested in the 17th century, however. Compare typologically Bulgarian гъстак (găstak), Macedonian густеж (gustež), Czech houští, Polish gęstwina (< *gǫstъ); Latin dūmus (akin to Latin dense).
examples: Suddenly from a lumpy tussock of old grass some twenty yards in front of them, with black-tipped ears erect and long hinder limbs throwing it forward, started a hare. It bolted for a thicket of alders.
He had to complete a thicket of paperwork before he was allowed to join the company.

senses: One who operates a bot (automated software process).
ety: From bot + -er.
examples: It is estimated by industry and leading botters that only around 1 in 10 players using bots make a profit, mainly in low-stakes games.

senses: The region of the uppermost atmosphere where the temperature increases along with the altitude due to the absorption of solar ultraviolet radiation by ozone.
ety: From French stratosphère, a word coined by its discoverer, meteorologist Léon Teisserenc de Bort. From strato- + -sphere.
examples: Variation in height of the stratosphere (isothermal layer).
Even if you’ve run an ironclad household budget and managed your retirement accounts on your own, you’re about to be at a level of wealth in a different stratosphere. It’s time to hire professionals.

senses: To wander around aimlessly, often causing irritation to others.
To beg, cadge, or sponge; to exploit or take advantage of others for personal gain.
To steal or filch.
ety: From Middle English moochen, mouchen (“to pretend poverty”), from Old French muchier, mucier, mucer (“to skulk, hide, conceal”), from Frankish *mukkjan (“to hide, conceal oneself”), from Proto-Germanic *mukjaną, *mūkōną (“to hide, ambush”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mūg-, *(s)mewgʰ- (“swindler, thief”). Cognate with Old High German mūhhōn (“to store, cache, plunder”), Middle High German muchen, mucken (“to hide, stash”), Middle English müchen, michen (“to rob, steal, pilfer”). More at mitch. Alternate etymology derives mooch from Middle English mucchen (“to hoard, be stingy”, literally “to
examples: These chaps that mooch about, as Hyde was doing, pick up all sorts of odds and ends. He may have pinched them from a chemist’s shop.

You have to be alone to mooch about properly. Other people will just get in the way and be all energetic about things. So wait until they've gone, make a cup of tea and then let the mooching commence.
With 79 minutes gone, the most celebrated team of the modern age had been reduced to bunch of mooching, stumbling yellow-shirted spectators.

senses: Besieged; surrounded by enemy troops.
Beset by trouble or difficulty.
ety: From beleaguer + -ed.
examples: Ministers have not ruled out stripping the beleaguered operator of its franchise when it comes up for renewal on October 16.

senses: The transport of goods by cart.
Any vehicular transportation of goods.
A charge made for such transport.
ety: From cart + -age.
examples: Railways are forming in one quarter of this earth, canals in another, much cartage is wanted
In these years, all long-distance freight went by rail, with local cartage by the railway's horses and carts.
I started general cartage work and hauling bagged cement to Pine Creek, south of Darwin.

senses: A small island.
ety: From Middle French islette. By surface analysis, is(le) + -let. Mostly displaced native Middle English eyt, eit and Middle English holm, holme (See eyot and holm for more).
examples: There is an islet on the other side of this body of water.

senses: A longfin tuna, a large marine fish (Thunnus alalunga) of warm seas, having edible flesh.
ety: From Portuguese albacor, from Arabic اَلْبَكُورَة (al-bakūra, “the young camels”).
examples: But most of all, they were jealous because these strangers feasted daily on great turtle, albacore and sail-fish, the sweetest of all seafoods.

senses: An instance of psyops: a psychological operation, usually of a clandestine sort.
Something viewed as inauthentic and pushing an agenda.
A psychological operative; a person who participates in psychological operations.
ety: Back-formation from psyops.
examples: The psyop wing of Disney’s marketing department is now so hair-raisingly effective that we can only wonder what will become of little girls imprinted so deeply with such cultish brand devotion.
Cynics saw an opportunist pandering to the gullible masses. Conspiracy theorists, of course, saw a CIA psyop.
If the Swift/Kelce pairing is a government psyop, as conservatives want to believe, the CIA sure knows how to stage damn good football.

senses: Solemnly or ponderously sad.
ety: From Middle English dolorous, from Old French dolerous (modern French douloureux), from Late Latin dolōrōsus (“painful”), from Latin dolor. Doublet of dolorose.
examples: Through dolorous despaire, which she conceyved, Into the Sea her selfe did headlong throw, Thinking to have her griefe by death bereaved.
From this prison here of horror, whence I every hour tend nearer and nearer to destruction, I send you . . . the assurance of my dolorous and unhappy service.
She turned and waved a hand to him, she cried a word, but he didn't hear it, it was a lost word. A sable wraith she was in the parkland, fading away into the dolorous crypt of winter.

senses: Erroneous in date; containing an anachronism; in a wrong time; not applicable to or not appropriate for the time.
ety: From anachronism + -ic.
examples: If you know where to look in the movie, you can spot an anachronistic wrist watch on one of the Roman soldiers.

The impiety of the Ciceronian attitude was probably his major objection to the sect, yet the dialogue is mainly concerned with the more anachronistic and illogical aspects of attempting to write only as Cicero did.
Among them, even the most lucid of 'one-nation' Tories had severe difficulties in seeing the anti-growth nature of some of the most anachronistic of traditional British institutions.

senses: A roundabout; traffic circle.
A road intersection, not necessarily circular in shape.
ety: Borrowed from Tagalog rotonda (“roundabout; traffic circle”).
examples: Welcome Rotonda is a roundabout located in Quezon City.
Pasay Rotonda is the intersection of EDSA and Taft Avenue, located in Pasay City.
Pasig Rotonda is the intersection of Pasig Boulevard and Dr. Sixto Antonio Avenue, located in Pasig City.

senses: A toasted manioc flour used in Brazilian cookery, typically as an accompaniment to a main meal.
ety: From Portuguese farofa, perhaps from Kimbundu falofa or from Latin far (“a type of hulled wheat”) + offa (“chunk; dumpling”).
examples: Farofa will be a part of any memorable Brazilian lunch, and it was of one in particular.

senses: Amorous; lustful.
ety: From Latin concupiscens (stem concupiscent-), present participle of concupīscō (“long for, covet”), inchoative of concupiō (“long for”), from con- + cupiō (“desire, wish for”).
examples: Call the roller of big cigars, / The muscular one, and bid him whip / In kitchen cups concupiscent curds.

senses: To congratulate.
ety: From Latin fēlicitātus, perfect passive participle of fēlīcitō (“to felicitate”) (from fēlīx (“happy”)), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French féliciter.
examples: Still, he tucked in handsomely to bacon and tomato on fried bread, felicitating himself on the considered wisdom of his arrival in the character of guest to Bradly.

senses: To twist one's body to and fro with short, writhing motions; to squirm.
To cause something to wriggle.
To use crooked or devious means.
ety: From wrig + -le (frequentative suffix). Compare Dutch wriggelen (“to wriggle, squirm”), Low German wriggeln (“to wriggle”). Related to Old English wrigian (“to turn, wend, hie, go move”), from Proto-Germanic *wrigōną (“to wriggle”).
examples: Teachers often lose their patience when children wriggle in their seats.
Both he and successors would often wriggle in their seats, as long as the cushion lasted.
I tried to ease my grip, but my hands were sweating so profusely that the lizards began to wriggle out of them.

senses: Somebody who is forced to stand up, for example, on a crowded bus.
A free-standing, rigid print, usually of a person or character (often life-sized), meant as a representation of a 3d object, commonly displayed for advertising and promotional purposes.
A board game piece made of upright cardboard inserted into a plastic base.
ety: From stand + -ee.
examples: He took a picture of me with a standee of Darth Vader at the premiere of Star Wars: Episode III.

I've always found the best thing to do with standees is to stick a small strip of clear tape to the edge of the cardboard that will be inserted into the stand. This prevents the shredding/tearing problem.

senses: A color print produced by chromolithography.
ety: Shortened from chromolithograph.
examples: All Nature is smiling, in fact, with one large, comprehensive smile, exactly like a first-class PRANG chromo with a fresh coat of varnish upon it.
It was manifest that we all felt that we ought to send the poor shoemaker SOMETHING. There was long and thoughtful discussion of this point; and we finally decided to send him a chromo.

senses: One who gives consolation.
ety: From console + -er.
examples: Grieving apparently wasn't a full-time job, however, since Hank up and married a gal named Billie Jean and daddied a daughter by yet another consoler.

senses: Of a place: having many trees.
ety: From woods + -y (suffix meaning ‘having the quality of’ forming adjectives), to distinguish the word from woody (“made of wood, or having wood-like properties, etc.”).
examples: No lovelier day, no woodsier woods, or better company.
If you simply must have a conifer, plant it as far from the house as possible, in the woodsiest corner of the yard, and select a native species.

senses: A sword having a blade made of a powerful beam of light or energy.
A real-world toy, prop, or device fashioned after the fictional lightsaber.
ety: From light + saber; coined by American filmmaker and philanthropist George Lucas for the Star Wars film franchise. First mentioned in the film Star Wars (later retitled Star Wars: Episode IV—A New Hope) which was released on May 25, 1977.
examples: Wielding his flashlight like a lightsaber, Kyle sent golden shafts slicing through the swirling vapors.

senses: An unskilled Asian worker, usually of Chinese or Indian descent; a labourer; a porter. Coolies were frequently transported to other countries in the 19th and early 20th centuries as indentured labourers.
ety: Borrowed from Hindustani (Hindi क़ुली (qulī) / Urdu قلی (qulī, “hired laborer”)), from Chagatai قلی (quli, “servant, slave”), ultimately from Proto-Turkic *kul. Another theory says that it is named after Gujarati કોળી (koḷī), a Gujarati tribe or caste. Other forms occur in Bengali কুলি (kuli) and Tamil கூலி (kūli, “daily hire”). Possibly also influenced by Hindustani (कोली (kolī) / کولی (kolī, “weaver; low-class”)), or Persian کول (kūl, “shoulder [upon which goods are hauled]”). In Kurdish Koile (کۆیلە) and Quli (قولى): Slave, Servant. Kawli (Keweli): Low-Class, Gypsy. Mandarin 苦力 (kǔlì, “hard
examples: One day when the Man's Wife and the Tertium Quid had just arrived in the Cemetery, they saw some coolies breaking ground.
Outside, beyond the sun-baked station yard, a rice mill chugged away in the distance, and sweating coolies unloaded bags of rice from creaking bullock carts.
Community histories did not necessarily feature the coolie, partly due to the fact that “coolie” is a classed term. Asian coolies were regarded as lowly laborers.

senses: Having a dark, bluish appearance.
Pale, pallid.
So angry that one turns pale; very angry; furious; liverish.
ety: From Middle English livid, livide, from Old French livide, from Latin līvidus (“bluish, livid; envious”), from līveō (“be of a bluish color or livid; envy”), from Proto-Italic *sliwēō, from Proto-Indo-European *sliwo-, suffixed form of *(s)leh₃y- (“bluish”). See also Old English slā (“sloe”), Welsh lliw (“splendor, color”), Old Irish li, Lithuanian slyvas (“plum”), and Russian and Old Church Slavonic слива (sliva, “plum”).
examples: When all the surroundings were thus rendered as brilliant as possible, so that the corpse looked more livid and ghastly by comparison, I seated myself once more, and prepared to read the last message of the dead.
The house seemed unfamiliar in the dark stormy light; the red and purple glass of the front door made livid bruises on the linoleum; the green chenille curtain was like a veil of seaweed.
I'm livid; a deathly pale light floods my face and I emanate a different smell. Charlie doesn't stop to analyse these subtle changes.

senses: A white person.
ety: The most likely earliest derivation is from the Wolof word for Europe, "Tougal". In the same way that Wolof means the people of Jollof, Toubab means the people of Tougal.
examples: Jean-Baptiste was my only real white friend in the trench. He was the only Toubab who came to console me after the death of Mademba Diop.

senses: To flow or cause to flow in a noisy series of spurts, as when liquid is emptied through the narrow neck of a bottle.
ety: Imitative; compare glug.
examples: But so long as the water kept flopping and glucking aside me, I was right.
The little phial glucked out its precious contents.
Know, O Commander of the Faithful, that the eldest of my brothers, he who became lame, is called Bakbuk because when he tattles he makes a glucking noise like water coming out of a jar.

senses: Constituting bait (something intended to allure), especially Oscar bait or clickbait.
ety: From bait (“something alluring”) + -y.
examples: Ginger is the latest, baitiest fashion that ever helped a girl make an impression . . . . in wonderful “Spartine” colors of black, brown, navy, cranberry, moss, red and blue.
Could it be almost too baity? It's ticking almost every Academy Award box going.
A far-right talking point had been turned into a clip with a baity headline, and attracted over 26,000 views.

senses: A chronological mistake; the erroneous dating of an event, circumstance, or object.
A person or thing which seems to belong to a different time or period of time.
The aberrant projection of the present onto the past.
ety: From New Latin anachronismus, from Ancient Greek ἀναχρονισμός (anakhronismós), from ἀναχρονίζομαι (anakhronízomai, “referring to the wrong time”), from ἀνά (aná, “up against”) + χρονίζω (khronízō, “spending time”), from χρόνος (khrónos, “time”). Analyzable as ana- + chrono- + -ism.
examples: You are too young—it is an anachronism for you to have such thoughts
His movements, his clothes, everything about him, seemed slightly out of place in this assembly. He spoiled the pattern; like Alvin, he was an anachronism.
We're also witnessing the passing of something even more profound - a culture of working-class masculinity that has become an anachronism in the modern world.

senses: A pointed tooth between the incisors and premolars in heterodont mammals.
ety: From Latin cuspid-, stem of cuspis (“point, apex”). Doublet of cusp and cuspis.
examples: Near-synonyms: eyetooth (only in humans); fang, fangtooth (particularly elongated cuspids in certain animals)

senses: An extra product given to a customer at no additional charge; a lagniappe.
ety: From Irish tuilleadh (“more”).
examples: A bakereen's dusind with tithe tillies to boot.

senses: Conveying knowledge, information or instruction.
ety: From instruct + -ive.
examples: Well, that was an instructive lesson.

senses: Of a position, privilege etc.: available for purchase rather than assigned on merit.
Capable of being bought (of a person); willing to take bribes.
Corrupt, mercenary.
ety: Borrowed from French vénal, from Old French venel, from Latin vēnālis (“for sale”), from vēnum (“something for sale”); compare English vend.
examples: Thus, regimental commands in the army were – as with the judiciary or the financial bureaucracy – venal posts, which were purchased, bequeathed and sold among the nobility.

senses: To go before, go in front of.
To cause to be preceded; to preface; to introduce.
To have higher rank than (someone or something else).
ety: From Middle French précéder, from Latin praecēdō, from prae- + cēdō.
examples: Cultural genocide precedes physical genocide.
But harm precedes not sin: onely our Foe / Tempting affronts us with his foul esteem / Of our integritie
This is the custom of sending on a basket-woman, who is to precede the pomp at a coronation, and to strew the stage with flowers, before the great personages begin their procession.

senses: To hem and haw.
To talk foolishly; to chatter.
ety: Borrowed from Scots haiver.
examples: This didn't seem at all unlikely, but when I none the less havered, he insisted that his 'Egyptian fortune-teller' had confirmed it.
To business, and no more havers.
And if I haver, Yeah I know I’m gonna be, I’m gonna be the man Who’s haverin' to you.

senses: Something, as a writing, that is of doubtful authorship or authority (formerly also used attributively).
ety: From Middle English apocrypha, apocrifa, apocrif, from Late Latin apocryphus (“secret, not approved for public reading”), from Ancient Greek ἀπόκρυφος (apókruphos, “hidden, obscure”, thus “(books) of unknown authorship”), from ἀπό (apó, “from”) + κρύπτω (krúptō, “to hide”). Properly plural (the singular would be apocryphon), but commonly treated as a collective singular. “Apocryphal” meaning “of doubtful authenticity” is first attested in English in 1590.
examples: But it may be objected, that these books being in the Jews' canon , ought to be acknowledged for divinely inspired , rather than the apocryphas that never were in it
We are the women with thread bags anchored deep in our bosoms containing blood agreements silver coins and cloves of garlic and an apocrypha of Nanny’s secrets.
The story of the Arsenal mural has drifted, over the years, into something more closely resembling a myth. What should be straightforward details are now shrouded in fog, tangled by apocrypha.

senses: Dizzy; swirling or moving as if seen in a daze.
ety: From swim + -y.
examples: I hadn't noticed at Peter Anderson's—my head was too swimmy to notice anything.

senses: A spy, undercover agent.
ety: From undercover.
examples: I've got mad hate for the undies Moving like gyal, tryna cuff me
Got a mind for the undies I'm tryna stay far from the pigs
